svg.aria-label: Wiring between TIDA-010083, LIFCL-40 FPGA and AR0234CS camera
svg.text: Wiring — TIDA-010083 · CrossLink-NX FPGA · AR0234CS camera
One CAT6 cable in, GigE Vision video out. The FPGA is the only device in the system that speaks both MIPI and Ethernet, so every signal crosses it.
PoE PD + DP83867IR GigE PHY · 27 × 27 mm
LIFCL-40-9BG400I
CrossLink-NX · caBGA-400 · 1.0 V core
onsemi AR0234CS
1920 × 1200 global shutter · ODCSP-83

g.text: needs no re-layout of this link.

svg.text: RJ45 · J4
What TIDA-010083 hands over
· 5 V ±2 %, up to 2.3 A — about 11 W after the PHY takes its share
· A complete 10/100/1000 PHY, already matched to the magnetics
· RGMII at 2.5 V, or any I/O voltage you like if R42 is removed
· Two isolated digital inputs and one isolated output on J4
· A 24 V auxiliary input that overrides PoE — invaluable on the bench
What it expects back
· PHY address and RGMII skew straps, fitted on your carrier
· An MDIO master to configure the PHY out of its defaults
· A MAC that respects the 200 ms / 195 µs register-access windows
· Controlled-impedance, length-matched RGMII on the carrier side
Why CrossLink-NX LIFCL-40
· Two hardened 4-lane D-PHY quads, 2.5 Gb/s per lane. No soft
D-PHY, no external resistor networks, no timing closure gamble.
· Wide-range banks take 1.2 / 1.5 / 1.8 / 2.5 / 3.3 V, so RGMII at
2.5 V connects with no level translation anywhere.
· Lattice specifically recommends RGMII over the SGMII-on-LVDS
path for gigabit Ethernet across the full temperature range —
which is exactly the interface TIDA-010083 exposes.
· 28 nm FD-SOI: low power and very low soft-error rate, both of
which matter in a sealed 29 mm housing with no airflow.
· DDR3L / LPDDR2 controller with x16 DQS for the frame buffer.
Why AR0234CS
· Global shutter — no skew on parts moving past the lens, which
is the entire point of a machine-vision camera.
· CSI-2 1.2 over 1, 2 or 4 lanes, 8 or 10 bit, 120 fps at full
resolution. Lane count is a configuration choice, not a redesign.
· Under 420 mW at the worst case — about 4 % of the PoE budget.
· Window control, binning and skipping in the sensor, so the
FPGA can trade resolution for frame rate without wasting bandwidth.
· Hardware TRIGGER in and FLASH out, which close the loop from
the isolated field input to the strobe with no software in the path.
· Accepts spread-spectrum EXTCLK, useful for EN 55011 class B.
Integration notes that decide whether this works first time

1 · Pick one RGMII delay source. Either put the DP83867 in Shift mode and dial the skew in 0.25 ns steps, or add ≥ 1.5 ns of clock trace on the carrier. Doing both breaks gigabit while 100 Mb/s still passes.

2 · Leave INT/PWDN floating from the FPGA side. It powers the PHY down if driven low, and it is an input until software says otherwise. Configure it as an input with an external 2.2 kΩ pull-up to +VIO.
3 · Fit the four-level strap dividers for PHY address and RGMII skew on the carrier, referenced to +VIO. The TIDA schematic says outright that this strapping is expected on the other board.
4 · Feed the camera's analogue rails from an LDO. The 4 MHz point-of-load switchers are excellent for logic and wrong for VAA and VAA_PIX, where ripple becomes visible banding.
5 · Budget FPGA configuration time against the PHY's 200 ms post-power-up window. The window starts when the rails come up, not when the FPGA finishes loading from flash.

6 · Route CSI-2 as 100 Ω differential pairs with tight intra-pair matching and a continuous reference plane. Keep them away from the 125 MHz RGMII group and from the switching nodes of every regulator.
7 · If the board must run standalone on the bench, feed 24 V into J4 — the auxiliary input takes priority above ≈15 V and bypasses PoE detection and classification entirely.
